CEILING.MATH_default_significance_1.description: Significance and mode both omitted -> defaults to nearest integer (significance 1). Source: Microsoft CEILING.MATH docs.

This is the modern, explicit-mode successor to legacy CEILING and was designed to match LibreOffice/ODF's CEILING(...,...,Mode) semantics for the default case.

CEILING.MATH_negative_mode_nonzero_away_.description: Negative number with a nonzero mode argument -> rounds away from zero instead of the toward-zero default.
CEILING.MATH_negative_mode_nonzero_away_.notes: Microsoft worked example: CEILING.MATH(-5.5,2,-1) = -6 ('rounds -5.5 down (away from 0) ... with a mode of -1'). Mode only affects negative numbers; any nonzero mode reverses the default direction.

CEILING_basic.description: Basic case, rounds 2.5 up to the nearest multiple of 1. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/ceiling-function-0a5cd7c8-0720-4f0a-bd2c-c943e510899f (worked example table)

CEILING_fractional_significance.description: Rounds 0.234 up to the nearest multiple of 0.01. Source: Microsoft CEILING docs worked example table.

CEILING_both_negative_away_from_zero.description: Number and significance both negative -> rounds away from zero (more negative), per Microsoft's documented rule and worked example.
CEILING_both_negative_away_from_zero.notes: Microsoft: 'If number is negative, and significance is negative, the value is rounded down, away from zero.' Worked example CEILING(-2.5,-2)=-4 at https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/ceiling-function-0a5cd7c8-0720-4f0a-bd2c-c943e510899f

CEILING_negative_number_positive_signifi.description: Number negative, significance positive -> rounds up toward zero (less negative), per Microsoft's documented rule and worked example.
CEILING_negative_number_positive_signifi.notes: Microsoft: 'If number is negative, and significance is positive, the value is rounded up towards zero.' Worked example CEILING(-2.5,2)=-2 at the same doc page.

CEILING_libreoffice_default_mode_diverge.description: GOLD QUIRK CANDIDATE: identical 2-argument call (Mode omitted) with number and significance both negative. Per Microsoft's documented CEILING rule this must round AWAY from zero.
CEILING_libreoffice_default_mode_diverge.notes: Microsoft (https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/ceiling-function-0a5cd7c8-0720-4f0a-bd2c-c943e510899f): both-negative case rounds away from zero, so CEILING(-45.67,-2) -> -46 (ratio -45.67/-2=22.835, ceiling(22.835)=23, 23*-2=-46). LibreOffice's own CEILING docs (https://help.libreoffice.org/latest/en-US/text/scalc/01/func_ceiling.html) define a 3rd optional Mode argument that ONLY applies when both Number and Significance are negative, and state: 'if Mode is equal to zero or not given, negative numbers are rounded up (towards zero)' -- with LO's own worked example CEILING(-45.67;-2;0) = -44. That means the identical 2-arg formula (Mode omitted) is documented to resolve to -44 under LibreOffice's own default, vs -46 under Microsoft's documented default -- a genuine cross-engine default-behavior divergence for the exact same formula text, not just a wording difference. If LO's executed result is -44, matched_expected:false here is the intended, correct signal of that divergence -- do not 'fix' this expectation to match LO.

FLOOR_fractional_significance.description: Rounds 0.234 down to the nearest multiple of 0.01. Source: Microsoft FLOOR docs worked example table.

FLOOR_both_negative_toward_zero.description: Number and significance both negative -> Microsoft's own worked example rounds this TOWARD zero (-2), which is the opposite direction CEILING takes for the same-signed case.
FLOOR_both_negative_toward_zero.notes: Microsoft's worked example table gives FLOOR(-2.5,-2) = -2 exactly (https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/floor-function-14bb497c-24f2-4e04-b327-b0b4de5a8886). Note this is the OPPOSITE rounding direction of CEILING(-2.5,-2)=-4 for the identical arguments -- FLOOR and CEILING deliberately diverge on both-negative inputs, not a bug.

FLOOR_mismatched_sign_error.description: Number positive, significance negative (opposite signs) -> #NUM!, explicitly documented by Microsoft: 'If Number is positive and Significance is negative, FLOOR returns the #NUM! error value.'

FLOOR_libreoffice_default_mode_divergenc.description: GOLD QUIRK CANDIDATE: mirror image of the CEILING default-Mode divergence. Both Number and significance negative, Mode omitted.
FLOOR_libreoffice_default_mode_divergenc.notes: Derived from Microsoft's own worked FLOOR(-2.5,-2)=-2 example (both-negative case rounds TOWARD zero): ratio -45.67/-2=22.835, truncating toward zero gives 22, 22*-2=-44. LibreOffice's own FLOOR docs (https://help.libreoffice.org/latest/en-US/text/scalc/01/func_floor.html) define an optional 3rd Mode argument that only applies when both Number and Significance are negative, stating 'Mode = 0 or omitted: negative numbers are rounded down (away from zero)' with LO's own worked example FLOOR(-45.67;-2;0) = -46. So the identical 2-arg formula (Mode omitted) is documented to resolve to -46 under LibreOffice's default vs -44 under Microsoft's documented behavior -- a genuine divergence, and the exact mirror image of the CEILING case above (there Excel defaults away-from-zero and LO defaults toward-zero; here Excel defaults toward-zero and LO defaults away-from-zero). If LO's executed result is -46, matched_expected:false is the correct, intended signal -- do not 'fix' this expectation to match LO.

FLOOR_nonnumeric_error.description: Nonnumeric first argument -> #VALUE!, per Microsoft docs: 'If either argument is nonnumeric, FLOOR returns the #VALUE! error value.'

MODE_basic_repeated_value.notes: This is Microsoft's own documented MODE example data set -- https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/mode-function-e45192ce-9122-4980-82ed-4bdc34973120 -- 4 appears 3 times, more than any other value

MROUND_mismatched_signs_error.description: Number and multiple must have the same sign, per Microsoft docs: 'The Number and Multiple arguments must have the same sign. If not, a #NUM error is returned.'

MROUND_zero.description: Zero rounds to zero regardless of the multiple.

MULTINOMIAL_two_groups.description: Ratio of the factorial of the sum to the product of factorials: 5!/(2!3!) = 10

NOMINAL_inverse_of_effect.description: Inverting EFFECT recovers the 6% nominal rate

NOT_zero_coercion.notes: Numeric coercion for logical functions confirmed via https://www.ablebits.com/office-addins-blog/excel-and-or-xor-not-functions/

NOT_nonzero_coercion.description: Any nonzero number coerces to TRUE, so NOT(5) -> FALSE

NOT_text_error.description: An arbitrary text literal cannot be coerced to a logical value -> #VALUE!

NOW_self_difference_is_deterministic.description: Two NOW() calls inside one cell evaluate in the same recalculation pass, so their difference is exactly 0 — a deterministic assertion about a volatile function (N() keeps the result a plain number instead of a duration-formatted cell)

NOW_on_or_after_today.description: NOW() includes today's date plus a time fraction, so it is always >= TODAY() within one recalculation

NPER_payoff_periods.description: Years to pay off 5000 at 10% with 1000/period: -ln(1-r*PV/pmt)/ln(1+r) = 7.2725

NUMBERVALUE_basic.description: Basic numeric text conversion with explicit US-style decimal_separator and group_separator arguments

NUMBERVALUE_malformed_text.description: Text that cannot be parsed as a number at all -> #VALUE!
NUMBERVALUE_malformed_text.notes: Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/numbervalue-function-1b05c8cf-2bfa-4437-af70-596c7ea7d879 - 'If any of the arguments are not valid, NUMBERVALUE returns the #VALUE! error value'

NUMBERVALUE_decimal_separator_used_twice.description: A decimal separator appearing more than once in the text is documented as invalid input -> #VALUE!

OCT2BIN_padded.description: The optional places argument pads the binary result to a fixed width

OCT2DEC_roundtrip.description: OCT2DEC reverses DEC2OCT, recovering the original number

ODD_round_up.description: Rounds up to the nearest odd integer

OFFSET_zero_offset_returns_same_cell.description: rows=0, cols=0 returns a reference to the exact starting cell

OR_range_numeric_all_zero.description: A range of all-zero numbers coerces to all-FALSE -> FALSE

PEARSON_perfect_negative.description: Perfectly linear, opposite-direction data gives a correlation of -1

POWER_negative_exponent.description: Negative exponent gives a reciprocal power

POWER_fractional_exponent_positive_base.description: Fractional exponent on a positive base is a well-defined real root (square root here)

POWER_negative_base_fractional_exponent.description: A negative base raised to a non-integer exponent has no real-number result in general (would require complex numbers), so Excel errors
POWER_negative_base_fractional_exponent.notes: Confirmed via Microsoft's own community support: entering =(-8)^(2/3) (equivalent power semantics to POWER) returns #NUM! in Excel -- https://answers.microsoft.com/en-us/msoffice/forum/all/excel-calculating-exponential-of-negative-number/5c67eae2-5682-4daf-b3d6-50b22e9919c2 -- note that -8^(1/3) is mathematically -2 as a real cube root, but Excel's POWER/^ implementation does not special-case rational exponents with odd integer denominators and returns #NUM! for any negative base with a non-integer exponent; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got -2

POWER_zero_to_zero.description: 0 raised to the 0th power; by the near-universal 'empty product' convention this is 1 (matches VBA's own '0^0', Python, C#, and LibreOffice/OpenOffice Calc)
POWER_zero_to_zero.notes: Real Excel (the worksheet function, and even the '^' operator) has a long-standing, Microsoft-acknowledged bug -- reproduced in Excel 2007 and 2010 and still reported unresolved -- where both '=0^0' and '=POWER(0,0)' incorrectly return #NUM! instead of 1, even though VBA's own 'x = 0 ^ 0' correctly evaluates to 1 in the same product. Recording the spec/cross-engine-consensus value (1) as 'expected' here so this exact Excel quirk shows up as a flagged divergence rather than being silently baked in as 'correct' -- https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/4850441/excel-formula-bug-00-gives-num

PPMT_first_month_principal.description: First-month principal: total payment 1798.65 minus 1500 interest

PROPER_apostrophe_word_boundary.description: PROPER treats an apostrophe as a word boundary too, capitalizing the letter that follows it -- so a name like o'brien becomes O'Brien. STANDARDIZE_below_mean.description: A value below the mean gives a negative z-score

STDEV.P_diverges_from_sample_same_data.description: Population standard deviation on the SAME dataset {2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9} used for STDEV/STDEV.S - divides by n instead of n-1, giving a smaller, exact result (2) vs the sample stdev's 2.138089935299395

STDEV.P_single_value_no_error.description: Unlike STDEV.S/STDEV, a single value does NOT error for the population formula, since it divides by n (=1), not n-1
STDEV.P_single_value_no_error.notes: Population variance of one point = 0/1 = 0, a valid result - genuine divergence from STDEV.S's #DIV/0! on the same single-cell input

STDEV.S_basic_two_points.description: Sample standard deviation of two hand-verifiable values, identical formula/data to STDEV_basic_two_points in the STDEV file

STDEV.S_matches_STDEV_same_data.description: STDEV.S on the classic Wikipedia sample dataset {2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9} - must match STDEV_matches_STDEV_S_same_data exactly, since STDEV.S is simply the Excel-2010+ modern name for the legacy STDEV calculation (same n-1 sample formula)

STDEV.S_single_value_div0.description: Sample stdev needs n>=2 (divides by n-1); one value -> #DIV/0!, confirmed against Microsoft's STDEV.S documentation of the n-1 method (https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/stdev-s-function-7d69cf97-0c1f-4acf-be27-f3e83904cc23)

STDEV_basic_two_points.description: Sample standard deviation of two hand-verifiable values

STDEV_matches_STDEV_S_same_data.description: Legacy STDEV on the classic Wikipedia sample dataset {2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9}; compare to STDEV.S_matches_STDEV_same_data on identical data in the STDEV.S file - both must return exactly the same value since STDEV.S is just the modern name for the same sample-stdev calculation

STDEV_single_value_div0.description: Sample stdev needs at least 2 data points (divides by n-1); a single value -> #DIV/0!
STDEV_single_value_div0.notes: n-1=0 with a single supplied value, causing division by zero

STDEVA_numbers_only.description: For pure numbers STDEVA equals STDEV (sample standard deviation)

STDEVA_counts_text_as_zero.description: Unlike STDEV, STDEVA counts text as 0, so {2,4,"x"} is treated as {2,4,0}: sample standard deviation 2

STDEVA_identical_values.description: Identical values have zero standard deviation

STDEVP_textbook.description: Population standard deviation of the classic 8-value example (mean 5, variance 4)

STDEVP_two_values.description: Two values equidistant from their mean of 3 give a population standard deviation of 1

STDEVP_ignores_text.description: Text and blank cells are ignored, not treated as zero

STDEVPA_textbook.description: For pure numbers STDEVPA equals STDEVP (population standard deviation): the classic example gives 2

SUBTOTAL_sum_code9.description: Function code 9 = SUM over visible rows (none hidden here)

SUBTOTAL_ignores_nested_subtotal.description: A5 contains its own SUBTOTAL over A1:A4; the outer SUBTOTAL must skip it (no double-count), so the answer is 100, not 200

SUM_basic_range.description: Basic sum of a contiguous numeric range

SUM_empty_range.description: Summing an entirely empty range returns 0, not an error

SUMIF_wildcard_text.description: Wildcard text criteria matches cells starting with 'a'

SUMIF_blank_cells_ignored.description: Blank cells interspersed in the range are simply skipped, not treated as matching or as errors

SUMIFS_basic.description: Sum of A where paired B > 2

SUMIFS_wildcard.description: Wildcard text criteria matches 2 of 3 rows

SUMPRODUCT_basic.description: Sum of pairwise products across two equal-sized arrays

SUMPRODUCT_single_array_acts_like_sum.description: With only one array argument, SUMPRODUCT just sums its elements

SUMPRODUCT_boolean_double_negative_count.description: Classic double-unary-minus idiom coerces a boolean array to 1/0 to count matches without an extra helper column
SUMPRODUCT_boolean_double_negative_count.notes: A3,A4,A5 satisfy >2; --(...) turns TRUE/FALSE into 1/0 and SUMPRODUCT sums them

SUMPRODUCT_condition_times_values_sumif_.description: Multiplying a boolean condition array by a value array replicates SUMIF without a separate criteria function
SUMPRODUCT_condition_times_values_sumif_.notes: Rows where A>2 (rows 3,4,5) contribute their B value: 30+40+50=120

SUMPRODUCT_mismatched_array_sizes_error.description: Arrays of different dimensions cannot be multiplied element-wise -> #VALUE!

TREND_extrapolate_exact_line.description: y=2x data extrapolated to x=5 must give exactly 10

TRIM_nonbreaking_space_not_removed.notes: Microsoft docs state explicitly: "by itself, the TRIM function does not remove the nonbreaking space character (which has a decimal value of 160 and is commonly used in web pages as the HTML entity  )." TRUE_equals_keyword.description: TRUE() returns a genuine logical value equal to the bare TRUE keyword

TRUE_in_if.description: TRUE() used as a condition behaves exactly like the TRUE keyword

TRUNC_basic_positive.description: Positive fractional number truncates its decimal part (same result as INT here)

TRUNC_negative_truncates_toward_zero.description: Documented classic divergence from INT: TRUNC simply removes the fractional part with no rounding, i.e. truncates TOWARD zero
TRUNC_negative_truncates_toward_zero.notes: Per Microsoft's TRUNC function docs, TRUNC(-8.9) = -8 (fractional part discarded, toward zero), whereas INT(-8.9) = -9 (rounds down, away from zero) -- see the paired INT_negative_rounds_toward_negative_infinity case in INT.json

TRUNC_num_digits_positive.description: num_digits=2 keeps two decimal places, discarding the rest without rounding
TRUNC_num_digits_positive.notes: 3.14159 truncated (not rounded) at 2 decimals is 3.14; if it were ROUND instead, 3.14159 would still round to 3.14 here, but TRUNC(3.145,2) vs ROUND(3.145,2) would diverge -- this case isolates the num_digits mechanic, not the rounding-vs-truncating distinction

TRUNC_negative_num_digits.description: Negative num_digits truncates digits to the LEFT of the decimal point
TRUNC_negative_num_digits.notes: Negative num_digits zeroes out the last 2 digits of the integer part without any rounding

TYPE_error.description: An error value -> code 16. TYPE classifies the error's TYPE rather than propagating the error itself, matching ISERROR-style special-casing

UNICHAR_accented_char.description: Basic code point beyond the 7-bit ASCII/basic-Latin range (U+00E9 'e with acute')

UNICHAR_roundtrip_via_unicode.description: Round trip: UNICODE() extracts the code point of an accented character, UNICHAR() converts it straight back
UNICHAR_roundtrip_via_unicode.notes: UNICODE(char) then UNICHAR(that number) must reproduce the original character exactly

UNICHAR_astral_emoji.description: Code point beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane (U+1F600 GRINNING FACE emoji), requiring a UTF-16 surrogate pair internally
UNICHAR_astral_emoji.notes: 128512 decimal = U+1F600, the grinning-face emoji; modern Excel supports supplementary-plane code points via surrogate pairs

UNICHAR_zero_error.description: UNICHAR(0) is documented to raise #VALUE! (0 is not a valid character code point). Verified via https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/unichar-function-ffeb64f5-f131-44c6-b332-5cd72f0659b8 ("Number: ... Numbers <=0 ... UNICHAR returns the #VALUE! error value")

UNICHAR_negative_error.description: Negative code point is out of range -> #VALUE! per the same UNICHAR documentation as UNICHAR_zero_error

UNICODE_accented_char.description: Code point of an accented character beyond basic Latin (U+00E9)

UNICODE_astral_emoji.description: Code point of a supplementary-plane emoji character (U+1F600), the inverse of the UNICHAR_astral_emoji case

UNICODE_empty_string_error.description: Empty text has no first character to inspect -> #VALUE!. Verified via https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/unicode-function-adb74aaa-a2a5-4dde-aff6-966e4e81f16f (documented error handling: invalid/partial character data returns #VALUE!)

UPPER_leaves_numbers_and_symbols.description: Digits and symbols have no case and are left unchanged

VALUE_currency_string.description: Currency formatting (symbol + thousands separator) is stripped during conversion; matches Microsoft's own VALUE documentation example

VALUE_non_numeric_string_error.description: A string that isn't a recognized number/date/time format -> #VALUE!

VAR.S_basic_two_points.description: Sample variance of two hand-verifiable values

VAR.S_wikipedia_dataset.description: Sample variance on the classic {2,4,4,4,5,5,7,9} dataset; this is the square of STDEV.S_matches_STDEV_same_data's result (2.138089935299395^2)

VAR_basic.description: Sample variance (divides by n-1) of three evenly spaced values

WEEKNUM_doc_example_monday_start_diverge.description: Same date as WEEKNUM_doc_example_default but return_type=2 (Monday-start): Microsoft's own docs show this returns a DIFFERENT week number (11, not 10) for the identical date -- the genuine return_type divergence
WEEKNUM_doc_example_monday_start_diverge.notes: Per Microsoft docs, WEEKNUM(3/9/2012,2) = 11, one more than the return_type=1 result of 10

WEEKNUM_return_type_21_is_iso_system.description: return_type 21 uses 'System 2': the week containing the year's first Thursday is week 1 (ISO 8601), a genuinely different algorithm from return_types 1/2/11-17 (all of which use 'week containing Jan 1 = week 1'). This should match ISOWEEKNUM(DATE(2023,1,1)) exactly -- see ISOWEEKNUM.json
WEEKNUM_return_type_21_is_iso_system.notes: Jan 1, 2023 is a Sunday; under the ISO rule it falls in the LAST ISO week (52) of 2022, not week 1 of 2023

WORKDAY_INTL_next_workday.description: 1 working day after Fri Jul 24 = Mon Jul 27 (default Sat/Sun weekend)

WORKDAY_basic_no_holidays.description: 5 working days after Mon Jan 1, 2024, no holidays supplied
WORKDAY_basic_no_holidays.notes: Jan 1, 2024 (Mon) + 5 workdays, skipping the Jan 6-7 weekend, = Jan 8, 2024 = serial 45299

WORKDAY_with_single_holiday.description: Same start/offset as WORKDAY_basic_no_holidays but with Jan 3 excluded as a holiday, pushing the result one calendar day later
WORKDAY_with_single_holiday.notes: With Jan 3 excluded, the 5th workday becomes Jan 9, 2024 = serial 45300

WORKDAY_multiple_holidays_via_range.description: holidays argument as a multi-cell range (Jan 3 and Jan 4 both excluded)
WORKDAY_multiple_holidays_via_range.notes: With both Jan 3 and Jan 4 excluded, the 5th workday becomes Jan 10, 2024 = serial 45301

WORKDAY_negative_days_goes_backward.description: Negative days argument counts backward from start_date instead of forward. Verified via https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/workday-function-f764a5b7-05fc-4494-9486-60d494efbf33 ("A positive value for days yields a future date; a negative value yields a past date")
WORKDAY_negative_days_goes_backward.notes: Jan 10, 2024 (Wed) - 5 workdays, skipping the Jan 6-7 weekend, = Jan 3, 2024 = serial 45294

WRAPCOLS_2.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 1, got '#NAME?'

WRAPROWS_2.description: Wrap a 4-cell row into a 2-column grid, filling by row
WRAPROWS_2.notes: MISMATCH vs expected: value mismatch: expected 1, got '#NAME?'

XIRR_one_year_10pct.description: -1000 on 2026-01-01, +1100 exactly 365 days later: annualized return is exactly 10% (dates given as serials)

XLOOKUP_exact_match.description: Basic exact-match lookup returns the corresponding value

XLOOKUP_not_found_default_na.description: No if_not_found arg and no match -> #N/A

XLOOKUP_not_found_custom.description: Custom if_not_found value is returned when no match

XLOOKUP_match_mode_next_smaller.description: match_mode -1 (exact or next smaller item) with no exact match
XLOOKUP_match_mode_next_smaller.notes: 2.5 has no exact match; next-smaller is 2 -> 20

XLOOKUP_search_mode_last_to_first.description: search_mode -1 finds the LAST occurrence of a duplicated key
XLOOKUP_search_mode_last_to_first.notes: Two rows match 'x' (1 and 3); reverse search returns the later one

XLOOKUP_empty_lookup_array.description: Degenerate 1-cell lookup/return arrays where the cell is blank
XLOOKUP_empty_lookup_array.notes: A1 and B1 are blank; lookup value 'a' is not found

XNPV_zero_at_irr.description: Discounting the same two dated cashflows at their XIRR (10%) must give NPV = 0

XOR_odd_count_of_true.description: An ODD number of TRUE arguments (3) -> TRUE

XOR_even_count_of_true.description: An EVEN number of TRUE arguments (2) -> FALSE, matching docs' own example =XOR(3>0,2<9) -> FALSE

XOR_zero_true_is_even.description: Zero TRUE arguments counts as even -> FALSE, matching docs' own example =XOR(3>12,4>6) -> FALSE

XOR_single_true.description: A single TRUE argument (odd count = 1) -> TRUE

XOR_range_numeric_coercion.description: Numbers in a range are coerced to logical (0=FALSE, nonzero=TRUE); here two nonzero values -> 2 TRUEs (even) -> FALSE

YEAR_of_date.description: YEAR applied to a constructed date

YEAR_of_raw_serial_epoch.description: YEAR applied directly to the raw serial number 1 (the classic Excel epoch, serial 1 = Jan 1, 1900)
YEAR_of_raw_serial_epoch.notes: Serial 1 is Jan 1, 1900 in the 1900 date system; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 1900, got 1899

YEAR_ignores_time_fraction.description: A serial with a fractional (time-of-day) component still resolves to the correct calendar year
YEAR_ignores_time_fraction.notes: 45366 = 2024-03-15; the .75 fractional day (18:00) is ignored by YEAR

YEARFRAC_basis0_us_nasd_default.description: Default basis 0 (US/NASD 30/360): treats every month as 30 days. Days = 6*30+29 = 209, over a 360-day year -> 209/360. Source: https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/office/yearfrac-function-3844141e-c76d-4143-82b6-208454ddc6a8 (worked example rounds to 0.58055556)

YEARFRAC_basis1_actual_actual.description: basis 1 (Actual/actual): actual 211 calendar days between the two dates, divided by 366 since the enclosing 1-year span (Jan 2012-Jan 2013) is a leap year. Source: Microsoft YEARFRAC docs worked example rounds to 0.57650273.
YEARFRAC_basis1_actual_actual.notes: 211/366 = 0.5765027322404372, matching Microsoft's documented rounded example (0.57650273) to 8 decimal places. Actual/actual leap-year-boundary handling is a documented high-divergence area across spreadsheet engines.

YEARFRAC_basis2_actual_360.description: basis 2 (Actual/360): actual 211 calendar days divided by a fixed 360-day year. Source: Microsoft YEARFRAC docs basis table.

YEARFRAC_basis3_actual_365.description: basis 3 (Actual/365): actual 211 calendar days divided by a fixed 365-day year. Source: Microsoft YEARFRAC docs worked example rounds to 0.57808219.
YEARFRAC_basis3_actual_365.notes: 211/365 = 0.5780821917808219, matches Microsoft's documented rounded example exactly.

YEARFRAC_basis4_european_30_360.description: basis 4 (European 30/360). For this particular date pair neither day-of-month is the 31st, so the European day-count adjustment never triggers and the result equals basis 0's 209/360.
YEARFRAC_basis4_european_30_360.notes: European 30/360 only differs from US 30/360 when a start/end day-of-month is 31; with day 1 and day 30 as here, both conventions compute 209/360 identically.

YEARFRAC_invalid_basis_error.description: basis values outside 0-4 are documented as invalid.
YEARFRAC_invalid_basis_error.notes: Microsoft docs: 'invalid basis values (< 0 or > 4) return a #NUM! error.'; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

AVERAGEA_documented_text_counts_as_zero.description: Microsoft's documented example: four numbers plus a text cell, where the text is averaged in as 0
AVERAGEA_documented_text_counts_as_zero.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 5.6 and explains it as 'The cell with the text "Not available" is used in the calculation', i.e. (10+7+9+2+0)/5. The text cell contributes a 0 AND is counted in the divisor, which is exactly how AVERAGEA differs from AVERAGE (AVERAGE would give 28/4 = 7). This worked example is what resolves the same text-vs-ignored contradiction that appears on the MAXA, MINA and VARPA pages

AVERAGEA_logicals_true_one_false_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: TRUE is counted as 1 and FALSE as 0, both counted in the divisor
AVERAGEA_logicals_true_one_false_zero.notes: Excel documents TRUE as 1 and FALSE as 0 for AVERAGEA: (1+1+0)/3 = 0.666666... -> 0.6667 at 4 dp. An engine using AVERAGE semantics (logicals in ranges ignored) would return 1

AVERAGEA_blank_cells_ignored.description: Empty cells are ignored entirely -- not counted as 0 and not counted in the divisor
AVERAGEA_blank_cells_ignored.notes: Microsoft's second worked example on the same page averages a range plus a separate cell and still returns 5.6 because the empty cell is not counted. Empty cells are ignored by AVERAGEA (only text and logicals are coerced), so the answer here is (10+20)/2 = 15, not (10+0+20)/3

AVERAGEA_all_text_range.description: A range containing only text averages the coerced zeros rather than erroring
AVERAGEA_all_text_range.notes: Under the documented 'array or reference arguments that contain text evaluate as 0' rule both cells count as 0 and both count in the divisor: (0+0)/2 = 0. Microsoft's page also states explicitly that empty text ("") evaluates as 0

AVERAGEA_no_data_points_div0.description: A range of only empty cells has no data points at all
AVERAGEA_no_data_points_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: Microsoft's AVERAGEA page documents no error condition. But it does document that empty cells are ignored, so a range of only empty cells leaves no data points and the average's divisor is zero -- #DIV/0! is the only consistent result

DOLLARDE_documented_sixteenths.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1 and 2/16 expressed in fractional notation converts to 1.125
DOLLARDE_documented_sixteenths.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.125. The fractional part .02 is read as 2 sixteenths: 1 + 2/16 = 1.125

DOLLARDE_documented_thirtyseconds.description: Documented example: 1.1 in thirty-seconds notation is 1 and 10/32
DOLLARDE_documented_thirtyseconds.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.3125. The fractional digits are padded to the width of the fraction denominator: .1 means 10 thirty-seconds, so 1 + 10/32 = 1.3125

DOLLARDE_non_integer_fraction_truncated.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: a non-integer fraction is documented as truncated to an integer
DOLLARDE_non_integer_fraction_truncated.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is not an integer, it is truncated.' Truncating 16.9 to 16 reproduces the first documented example exactly, 1.125. An engine that rounded 16.9 to 17, or used it as-is, would return a different value

DOLLARDE_negative_dollar_value.description: A negative fractional dollar keeps its sign through the conversion
DOLLARDE_negative_dollar_value.notes: The magnitude converts the same way as the documented positive example and the sign is preserved: -(1 + 2/16) = -1.125

DOLLARDE_zero_fraction_div0.description: A fraction denominator of zero cannot be divided by
DOLLARDE_zero_fraction_div0.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is greater than or equal to 0 and less than 1, DOLLARDE returns the #DIV/0! error value.' Note the band is 0 <= fraction < 1, which is worded more widely than DOLLARFR's page (which names only fraction = 0) even though truncation makes the two equivalent in practice; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#DIV/0!', got '#VALUE!'

DOLLARDE_negative_fraction_num_error.description: A negative fraction denominator is outside the documented domain
DOLLARDE_negative_fraction_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if fraction is less than 0; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

DOLLARFR_documented_sixteenths.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1.125 decimal converts to 1.02, read as 1 and 2/16
DOLLARFR_documented_sixteenths.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.02. 0.125 * 16 = 2 sixteenths, written in the fractional notation as .02

DOLLARFR_documented_thirtyseconds.description: Documented example: the same decimal in thirty-seconds is 1.04, read as 1 and 4/32
DOLLARFR_documented_thirtyseconds.notes: Excel documents this example's result as 1.04. 0.125 * 32 = 4 thirty-seconds, written as .04

DOLLARFR_round_trips_dollarde.description: DOLLARFR is documented as the inverse of DOLLARDE, so a round trip returns the original notation
DOLLARFR_round_trips_dollarde.notes: DOLLARDE(1.02,16) = 1.125 and DOLLARFR(1.125,16) = 1.02, so the composition is the identity on this value

DOLLARFR_non_integer_fraction_truncated.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: a non-integer fraction is documented as truncated to an integer
DOLLARFR_non_integer_fraction_truncated.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is not an integer, it is truncated.' 16.9 truncates to 16, so the answer must match the first documented example, 1.02

DOLLARFR_zero_fraction_div0.description: A fraction denominator of zero is a division by zero
DOLLARFR_zero_fraction_div0.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'If fraction is 0, DOLLARFR returns the #DIV/0! error value.' The DOLLARDE page words the same condition as the wider band 0 <= fraction < 1; because fraction is truncated first the two are equivalent, but the published wording differs between the pages; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#DIV/0!', got '#VALUE!'

DOLLARFR_negative_fraction_num_error.description: A negative fraction denominator is outside the documented domain
DOLLARFR_negative_fraction_num_error.notes: Excel documents #NUM! if fraction is less than 0; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#NUM!', got '#VALUE!'

FVSCHEDULE_documented.description: Microsoft's documented example: 1 unit of principal compounded at 9%, 11% then 10%
FVSCHEDULE_documented.notes: Microsoft publishes this example (=FVSCHEDULE(1,{0.09,0.11,0.1})) with the result displayed as 1.3309. The documented computation -- principal times the product of (1+rate) over the schedule -- is exact here: 1 * 1.09 * 1.11 * 1.10 = 1.330890 with no rounding, so 1.33089 is asserted at 7 dp rather than the page's 4-dp display

FVSCHEDULE_principal_scaled.description: The schedule is applied multiplicatively to any principal

FVSCHEDULE_empty_cell_is_zero_rate.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: Excel documents empty cells in the schedule as zeros (a 0% period), not as skipped
FVSCHEDULE_empty_cell_is_zero_rate.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'The values in schedule can be numbers or blank cells; any other value produces the #VALUE! error value for FVSCHEDULE. Blank cells are taken as zeros (no interest).' So the blank is a 0% period: 1000 * 1.1 * 1.0 * 1.1 = 1210. An engine that silently skipped the blank would get the same answer here, but an engine that errored on the blank would not -- so this pins the documented 'blank means 0%' rule

FVSCHEDULE_negative_rate.description: A negative rate in the schedule shrinks the principal

FVSCHEDULE_text_in_schedule_error.description: Non-numeric values in the schedule are an error, not a zero
FVSCHEDULE_text_in_schedule_error.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft: 'any other value produces the #VALUE! error value for FVSCHEDULE'. Note this is the opposite of most statistical functions, which ignore stray text in a reference, and it differs from an empty cell, which the same sentence documents as a zero rate; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#VALUE!', got 1.09

ISPMT_documented_first_month.description: Microsoft's documented example: interest paid in the first month of an 8,000,000 loan at 10% over three years
ISPMT_documented_first_month.notes: Microsoft's ISPMT page publishes no formula and no text example (its worked example is an image), and it contradicts itself on indexing: the argument table says per 'must be between 1 and Nper' while Remarks says 'ISPMT counts each period beginning with zero, not with one'. The even-principal formula ISPMT = pv * rate * (per/nper - 1) is confirmed by LibreOffice's own documented example (see the ISPMT_libreoffice_documented_example case) and reproduces Microsoft's own published figure of -64,814.8148 here: 8000000 * (0.1/12) * (1/36 - 1) = -64814.81481. Negative because it is cash paid out

ISPMT_documented_first_year.description: Documented example: interest paid in the first year of the same loan on an annual schedule
ISPMT_documented_first_year.notes: Same formula on an annual schedule: 8000000 * 0.1 * (1/3 - 1) = -533333.3333, matching the -533,333.33 figure published for this example

ISPMT_last_period_is_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: at per = nper the remaining balance is zero, so the interest is exactly zero
ISPMT_last_period_is_zero.notes: The documented formula pv*rate*(per/nper - 1) gives 8000000*0.1*(3/3 - 1) = 0. This is the clearest test of ISPMT's period indexing: an engine that treats per as 0-based, or that uses (1 - per/nper) with the opposite sign convention, will not return 0 here

ISPMT_period_zero_is_full_interest.description: At per = 0 the whole principal is still outstanding, so the interest is the full period charge
ISPMT_period_zero_is_full_interest.notes: 8000000 * 0.1 * (0/3 - 1) = -800000, i.e. one period's interest on the undiminished balance

ISPMT_libreoffice_documented_example.description: Cross-vendor check: LibreOffice's help page publishes a worked example for the same function
ISPMT_libreoffice_documented_example.notes: LibreOffice's Calc help documents ISPMT(Rate; Period; TotalPeriods; Invest) with the worked example =ISPMT(1%;18;24;120000) = -300. That is exactly pv * rate * (per/nper - 1) = 120000 * 0.01 * (18/24 - 1) = -300, so both vendors' documentation agrees on the formula and on the sign convention

ISPMT_zero_nper_div0.description: A zero number of periods divides by zero inside the per/nper term
ISPMT_zero_nper_div0.notes: DERIVED, not quoted: Microsoft's ISPMT page documents no error conditions at all. The formula confirmed by both vendors' worked examples divides per by nper, so nper = 0 is a division by zero and #DIV/0! is the consistent result; MISMATCH vs expected: expected '#DIV/0!', got '#NUM!'

KURT_documented_sample.description: Microsoft's documented example: kurtosis of the ten-value sample 3,4,5,2,3,4,5,6,4,7
KURT_documented_sample.notes: Excel documents this example's result as -0.1518. Independently derived from the documented excess-kurtosis formula n(n+1)/((n-1)(n-2)(n-3)) * SUM(((x-mean)/s)^4) - 3(n-1)^2/((n-2)(n-3)) with n = 10, mean 4.3, s = 1.4181 -> -0.15179964

KURT_leptokurtic_outlier_positive.description: A heavy single outlier raises kurtosis above zero
KURT_leptokurtic_outlier_positive.notes: Derived from the documented formula: mean 2.6, s = 3.5777; standardized deviations are four copies of -0.44721 and one of 1.78885; sum of 4th powers = 10.4; n(n+1)/((n-1)(n-2)(n-3)) = 30/24 = 1.25; 1.25*10.4 = 13; minus 3(n-1)^2/((n-2)(n-3)) = 48/6 = 8; 13-8 = 5

KURT_fewer_than_four_points_div0.description: The (n-3) factor is undefined below four data points
KURT_fewer_than_four_points_div0.notes: Excel documents #DIV/0! if there are fewer than four data points, because (n-3) is zero

KURT_zero_variance_div0.description: Identical values give a zero sample standard deviation
KURT_zero_variance_div0.notes: Excel documents #DIV/0! if the sample standard deviation of the data is zero

LENB_ascii_string.description: Microsoft's documented example string: byte length of an 11-character ASCII string
LENB_ascii_string.notes: Microsoft's LEN/LENB page uses 'Phoenix, AZ' as its worked example and publishes LEN = 11. The DBCS rule (see the LENB_non_ascii_characters case) cannot change the answer here because every character is single-byte under either reading. NOTE: the current live page now states 'The LENB function is deprecated' and has dropped the DBCS explanation entirely

LENB_empty_string.description: An empty string has zero bytes
LENB_empty_string.notes: No characters means no bytes, under either the DBCS or the non-DBCS rule

LENB_counts_trailing_spaces.description: Spaces are characters and are counted, including leading and trailing ones
LENB_counts_trailing_spaces.notes: Microsoft documents 'Spaces count as characters' for the text argument of LEN/LENB; the string here is two spaces, three letters and three spaces = 8

LENB_number_argument_coerced.description: A numeric argument is converted to its text representation before measuring
LENB_number_argument_coerced.notes: The number 1234 becomes the four-character string "1234", so the byte length is 4 in a non-DBCS default language

LENB_non_ascii_characters.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: two CJK characters, where the byte count depends on the DBCS language rule
LENB_non_ascii_characters.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft's archived LEN/LENB page: 'LENB counts 2 bytes per character only when a DBCS language is set as the default language. Otherwise LENB behaves the same as LEN, counting 1 byte per character', with DBCS listed as Japanese, Chinese (Simplified/Traditional) and Korean. The harness runs under a non-DBCS default locale, so the documented answer is 2 (LEN semantics). An engine that always counts raw UTF-8 or UTF-16 bytes returns 6 or 4 instead -- recording which one each engine does is the point of this case; MISMATCH vs expected: expected 2, got 4

LENB_propagates_error.description: An error argument propagates instead of being measured
LENB_propagates_error.notes: The argument evaluates to #DIV/0! before LENB sees it, so the error is the result

MAXA_documented_logical_beats_numbers.description: Microsoft's documented example: the largest value in a range where TRUE is counted as 1
MAXA_documented_logical_beats_numbers.notes: Excel documents MAXA as evaluating a logical TRUE in a range as 1, so the answer is 1 rather than 0.5; MAX over the same range would return 0.5 because MAX ignores logicals in ranges

MAXA_text_in_range_counts_as_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: all-negative numbers plus a text cell -- Excel counts the text as 0, which becomes the maximum
MAXA_text_in_range_counts_as_zero.notes: Microsoft's MAXA page carries two remarks that contradict each other for this exact input: 'Arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0 (zero)' and, one line later, 'Empty cells and text values in the array or reference are ignored'. We assert the text-evaluates-as-0 reading, because AVERAGEA's page carries the identical contradictory pair and settles it with a worked example (28/5 = 5.6) in which range text counts as 0. Under that reading the answer is 0 (0 > -3); under the 'ignored' reading it would be -3. The point of this case is to record which reading each engine actually implements

MAXA_false_in_range_counts_as_zero.description: FALSE in a range is evaluated as 0, so it wins over negative numbers
MAXA_false_in_range_counts_as_zero.notes: Excel documents logical FALSE as 0 for MAXA; 0 > -1 so the maximum is 0

MAXA_direct_logical_argument.description: A logical typed directly as an argument is also coerced (TRUE -> 1)
MAXA_direct_logical_argument.notes: Excel documents that MAXA evaluates TRUE as 1 whether it comes from a range or is typed as an argument

MAXA_blank_cells_ignored.description: Truly empty cells are ignored (they are not counted as 0)
MAXA_blank_cells_ignored.notes: Excel documents empty cells in a reference as ignored by MAXA (this remark is not contradicted elsewhere on the page, unlike the text remark), so the maximum is the largest actual number, -2, and NOT 0

MAXA_direct_text_argument_counts_as_zero.description: A non-numeric string typed directly as an argument is documented as evaluating to 0, which then wins
MAXA_direct_text_argument_counts_as_zero.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft's MAXA page: 'Arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0 (zero)'. Under that rule the literal "abc" becomes 0, which is larger than -5. (MAX's page carries the opposite rule -- text that cannot be translated into numbers causes an error -- so this case checks that an engine applies the A-variant rule and not MAX's)

MAXA_error_value_propagates.description: An error value passed as an argument propagates instead of being coerced
MAXA_error_value_propagates.notes: Error values are not among the things MAXA coerces; NA() produces #N/A and that error is the result of the whole expression

MINA_documented_false_is_smallest.description: Microsoft's documented example: FALSE in the range evaluates to 0, which is the smallest value
MINA_documented_false_is_smallest.notes: Microsoft's worked example for this exact data returns 0, explained on the page as 'Because a value of FALSE evaluates to 0, it is the smallest'. MIN over the same range would return 0.2, because MIN ignores logicals in a reference

MINA_text_in_range_counts_as_zero.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: all-positive numbers plus a text cell -- Excel counts the text as 0, which becomes the minimum
MINA_text_in_range_counts_as_zero.notes: Microsoft's MINA page carries the same self-contradicting pair as MAXA ('text ... evaluate as 0' vs 'text values in the array or reference are ignored'). We assert the text-evaluates-as-0 reading, which AVERAGEA's worked example confirms for the identical wording. Under that reading the answer is 0 (0 < 3); under the 'ignored' reading it would be 3. This case records which reading the engine implements

MINA_true_only_range.description: A range of logical TRUEs is a range of 1s
MINA_true_only_range.notes: Both cells evaluate to 1, so the minimum is 1

MINA_blank_cells_ignored.description: Truly empty cells are ignored rather than counted as 0
MINA_blank_cells_ignored.notes: Excel documents empty cells as ignored by MINA; if blanks counted as 0 the answer would be 0, so this distinguishes blank handling from text handling

MINA_direct_text_argument_counts_as_zero.description: A non-numeric string typed directly as an argument is documented as evaluating to 0, which then wins
MINA_direct_text_argument_counts_as_zero.notes: Verbatim from Microsoft's MINA page: 'Arguments that contain text or FALSE evaluate as 0 (zero)'. Under that rule the literal "abc" becomes 0, which is smaller than 5. MIN's page carries the opposite rule, so this case checks the A-variant rule is applied

MINA_error_value_propagates.description: An error value passed as an argument propagates instead of being coerced
MINA_error_value_propagates.notes: Error values are not coerced by MINA; NA() produces #N/A and that error is the result

MIRR_documented_five_years.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 5 years of cash flows, 10% finance rate, 12% reinvestment rate
MIRR_documented_five_years.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 12.61% (the live page displays it rounded to 13%). Independently derived from the documented formula MIRR = (-NPV(reinvest, positives)*(1+reinvest)^n / (NPV(finance, negatives)*(1+finance)))^(1/(n-1)) - 1 with n = 6 values: the reinvested inflows are carried forward at 12% and the single -120000 outflow discounted at 10%; the 5th root of the ratio gives 0.12609413 -> 0.1261 at 4 dp

MIRR_documented_first_three_years.description: Same doc example truncated to the first three years of inflows, which is still a net loss
MIRR_documented_first_three_years.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as -4.80% (displayed rounded to -5%). Same formula with n = 4 values (-120000, 39000, 30000, 21000): the reinvested inflows do not recover the outflow, so the cube root of the ratio is below 1 -> -0.04804466 -> -0.048 at 4 dp

MIRR_documented_reinvest_14pct.description: Same cash flows with the reinvestment rate raised from 12% to 14%
MIRR_documented_reinvest_14pct.notes: Microsoft publishes this example's result as 13.48% (displayed rounded to 13%). Raising only the reinvestment rate raises the future value of the positive flows; recomputing the documented formula gives 0.13475911 -> 0.1348 at 4 dp

MIRR_zero_flow_in_series.description: A zero cash flow is neither an inflow nor an outflow, so it only contributes to the period count
MIRR_zero_flow_in_series.notes: Excel documents that MIRR ignores text, logical values and empty cells in a reference but INCLUDES cells with the value zero. Zero belongs to neither the positive nor the negative NPV; with finance = reinvest = 0.1, the future value of the inflows is 600*1.1 + 700 = 1360 and the compounded present value of the outflow is -1000, with n = 4 values, so (1360/1000)^(1/3) - 1 = 0.10793165 -> 0.1079

MIRR_no_negative_value_div0.description: Excel documents #DIV/0! when values contains no negative (or no positive) number

VAR.P_documented_population_variance.description: Microsoft's documented breaking-strength example: population variance of ten tool readings

VAR.P_ignores_text_in_range.description: DIVERGENCE PROBE: the paired case to VARPA -- VAR.P IGNORES text rather than counting it as 0

VAR.P_single_value_is_zero.description: One data point has zero population variance

VAR.P_no_numeric_values_div0.description: A range holding only text leaves VAR.P with no data points

VARPA_documented_population_variance.description: Microsoft's documented breaking-strength example: population variance of ten numeric readings

VARPA_single_value_is_zero.description: Population variance of a single data point is defined (0), unlike sample variance

VARPA_empty_range_div0.description: With no data points at all there is nothing to divide by

COPILOT_exists_probe.notes: NOT ASSERTABLE BY DESIGN, and deliberately recorded as a probe rather than a support claim. COS_doc_radians.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the cosine of 1.047 radians
COS_doc_radians.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5001711. Independently derived: math.cos(1.047) = 0.5001710745970701 -> 0.5001711 at 7 dp. 1.047 is a decimal approximation of pi/3, which is why the result sits just above 0.5

COS_doc_degrees_via_pi.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: 60 degrees converted to radians by multiplying by PI()/180
COS_doc_degrees_via_pi.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5, and cos(60 degrees) = cos(pi/3) = 1/2 exactly. In IEEE double arithmetic math.cos(math.pi/3) evaluates to 0.5000000000000001, one unit in the last place above 0.5, so the assertion is made at 9 dp where the exact and floating-point values agree

COS_doc_degrees_via_radians_fn.description: Microsoft's documented worked example: the same 60 degrees converted with the RADIANS function instead
COS_doc_degrees_via_radians_fn.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 0.5 as well. COS_at_zero.notes: Follows from the definition of the cosine, cos(0) = 1 exactly, with no rounding needed: this anchors the function at a point where any floating-point implementation must be exact

CRITBINOM_doc_example.notes: Microsoft's page publishes this example's result as 4. Independently derived by summing the binomial probabilities explicitly: with trials 6 and probability 0.5 the cumulative sums are 0.015625, 0.109375, 0.34375, 0.65625, 0.890625, 0.984375, 1.0 for k = 0..6. The criterion 0.6 was chosen precisely because it discriminates: with 7 trials the sums are 0.0078125, 0.0625, 0.2265625, 0.5, 0.7734375, ... and the first >= 0.6 is at k = 4, so an engine that rounded 6.9 up to 7 instead of truncating would return 4 here. CUBEKPIMEMBER_no_cube_connection_probe.description: Existence probe only: the KPI-member form from Microsoft's own example, against a connection name that does not exist in this workbook. No OLAP connection can exist in a flat workbook, so this records what the engine actually returns rather than asserting a documented value
CUBEKPIMEMBER_no_cube_connection_probe.notes: NOT EXECUTABLE AS DOCUMENTED, and deliberately recorded as a probe rather than a support claim. Microsoft documents this function as returning data from an OLAP cube reached through a named workbook connection -- the CUBEKPIMEMBER page states outright that the cube functions are "supported only when the workbook is connected to a Microsoft SQL Server 2005 Analysis Services or later data source". A flat .xlsx carries no such connection, and neither LibreOffice Calc nor Google Sheets can supply one, so the documented behaviour cannot be reproduced by this harness in any engine. Microsoft's page documents that "if the connection name is not a valid workbook connection stored in the workbook, CUBEKPIMEMBER returns a #NAME? error value", and the same for an OLAP server that is not running. The trap this case exists to avoid: Excel itself documents that an invalid connection name yields #NAME?, which is the SAME token an engine emits for a function it has never heard of. A #NAME? here therefore does NOT distinguish "present but unconnected" from "absent", and this case is recorded with no asserted expected value so it can never be scored as documented behaviour. What the run does establish is recorded separately: probing all four pinned LibreOffice builds (24.2.0.3, 24.8.7.2, 25.2.0.3, 25.8.7.3) with the plain name, the _xlfn. storage form and the COM.MICROSOFT. add-in form returned #NAME? for all three spellings on every build, which is the signature of a name the engine does not implement at all rather than of a missing data connection
